Beware--</hi>Greek, "Have your eye on" so as to beware of. Contrast "mark," or "observe," namely, so as to follow <reference osisRef="Phil.3.17">Php 3:17</reference>.<div eID="gen36041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36042" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dogs--</hi>Greek, "the dogs," namely, those impure persons "of whom I have told you often" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.18">Php 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">19</reference>); "the abominable" (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.21.8">Re 21:8</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">Re 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.6">Mt 7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>): "dogs" in filthiness, unchastity, and snarling (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.18">De 23:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.59.6">Psa 59:6</reference>, 14, 15; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.22">2Pe 2:22</reference>): especially "enemies of the cross of Christ" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.18">Php 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.20">20</reference>). The Jews regarded the Gentiles as "dogs" (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.26">Mt 15:26</reference>); but by their own unbelief they have ceased to be the true Israel, and are become "dogs" (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.56.10">Is 56:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen36042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">evil workers--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Cor.11.13">2Co 11:13</reference>), "deceitful workers." Not simply "evildoers" are meant, but men who "worked," indeed, ostensibly for the Gospel, but worked for evil: "serving not our Lord, but their own belly" (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.16.18">Ro 16:18</reference>). Translate, "The evil workmen," that is, bad teachers (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.15">2Ti 2:15</reference>).<div eID="gen36043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36044" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">concision--</hi>Circumcision had now lost its spiritual significance, and was now become to those who rested on it as any ground of justification, a senseless mutilation. Christians have the only true circumcision, namely, that of the heart; legalists have only "concision," that is, the cutting off of the flesh. To make "cuttings in the flesh" was expressly prohibited by the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.5">Le 21:5</reference>): it was a Gentile-heathenish practice (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.28">1Ki 18:28</reference>); yet this, writes Paul indignantly, is what these legalists are virtually doing in violation of the law. There is a remarkable gradation, says Birks [Horæ Apostolicæ] in Paul's language as to circumcision. In his first recorded discourse (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.39">Ac 13:39</reference>), circumcision is not named, but implied as included in the law of Moses which cannot justify. Six or seven years later, in the Epistle to Galatians (<reference osisRef="Gal.3.3">Ga 3:3</reference>), the first Epistle in which it is named, its spiritual inefficiency is maintained against those Gentiles who, beginning in the Spirit, thought to be perfected in the flesh. Later, in Epistle to Romans (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.28">Ro 2:28</reference>, 29), he goes farther, and claims the substance of it for every believer, assigning the shadow only of it to the unbelieving Jew. In Epistle to Colossians (<reference osisRef="Col.2.11">Col 2:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.11">3:11</reference>), still later, he expounds more fully the true circumcision as the exclusive privilege of the believer. Last of all here, the very name is denied to the legalist, and a term of reproach is substituted, "concision," or flesh-cutting. Once obligatory on all the covenant-people, then reduced to a mere national distinction, it was more and more associated in the apostle's experience with the open hostility of the Jews, and the perverse teaching of false brethren. <div eID="gen36044" type="x-p"/>

Once lost, I have been "found," and I hope to be perfectly "found" by Him (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.8">Lu 15:8</reference>).<div eID="gen36068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen36069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">own righteousness ... of the law--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Phil.3.6">Php 3:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Ro 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.5">5</reference>). Paul was transported from legal bondage into Christian freedom at once, and without any gradual transition. Hence, the bands of Pharisaism were loosed instantaneously; and opposition to Pharisaic Judaism took the place of opposition to the Gospel. Thus God's providence fitly prepared him for the work of overthrowing all idea of legal justification. "The righteousness of faith," in Paul's sense, is the righteousness or perfect holiness of Christ appropriated by faith, as the objective ground of confidence for the believer, and also as a new subjective principle of life. Hence it includes the essence of a new disposition, and may easily pass into the idea of sanctification, though the two ideas are originally distinct. It is not any arbitrary act of God, as if he treated as sinless a man persisting in sin, simply because he believes in Christ; but the objective on the part of God corresponds to the subjective on the part of man, namely, faith. The realization of the archetype of holiness through Christ contains the pledge that this shall be realized in all who are one with Him by faith, and are become the organs of His Spirit. "The prize" is "the crown of righteousness" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">1Co 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>). <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Re 2:10</reference>, "crown of life." <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1Pe 5:4</reference>, "a crown of glory that fadeth not away."
